indicator.subject: History
indicator.sub_strand: Why and How We Study History
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.1. Demonstrate understanding of what history is about and how it is part of everyday life.
indicator.objective: Explain that history deals with past human activities

skills.description: Distinguish a completed human action from a plan.
Identify who acted and what the person did.
Place two events in time order.
Recount something that happened using a detail from the event.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: A plan describes what may happen tomorrow.
The gate tells where the welcome happened.
Eating came after washing in Ama's story.
A hope tells what we want to happen.

questions.stem: Which tells about something a person already did?
hints: Look for something that has happened.
questions.explanation: Yesterday comes before today. The singers have already done the activity.
questions.misconception: A plan describes what may happen tomorrow.

A plan describes what may happen tomorrow.
A request asks for an action later.
distractorMisconceptions.Can we sing next week?: A question about next week does not report a past event.

questions.stem: Which word helps show that a race is over?
hints: When did the runners finish?
questions.explanation: Yesterday points back to an earlier day. An event on that day is in the past.
questions.misconception: Tomorrow comes after today.

distractorMisconceptions.Soon: Soon refers to something still to happen.

questions.stem: Tell a partner one thing you did before school today.
hints: Think about getting ready to come to class.
questions.explanation: A child might say that they packed their bag. Packing came before the lesson.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Makes clear that the action is over.

criteria.description: Names a real completed action.
Makes clear that the action is over.

questions.stem: Draw a picture of someone doing an activity you saw yesterday. Tell what happened.
hints: Think who was there and what they did.
questions.explanation: A picture of a friend sweeping can help you tell how the friend cleaned the room yesterday.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Describes the action as something seen earlier.

criteria.description: Shows a person carrying out an action.
Describes the action as something seen earlier.

questions.stem: A pupil says all history happened long before anyone in our class was born. Give a different example.
hints: Remember an earlier day at school.
questions.explanation: A past class visit is part of the class’s history even if the visit was recent.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains that it already happened.

criteria.description: Uses an event from the learner’s lifetime.
Explains that it already happened.

questions.stem: In the story “Our teacher welcomed us at the gate”, who did the welcoming?
hints: Find the person who did the action.
questions.explanation: The teacher is the person named. Welcoming the pupils was the teacher’s activity.
questions.misconception: The gate tells where the welcome happened.

distractorMisconceptions.The gate: The gate tells where the welcome happened.
distractorMisconceptions.The school bag: A bag is something a pupil carries.
distractorMisconceptions.The bell: A bell is an object, not the person who welcomed us.

questions.stem: Which note tells both who acted and what they did?
hints: Look for a person and an action together.
questions.explanation: Abena is the person. Ringing the bell tells what she did.
questions.misconception: This names the object but leaves out who used it.

This names the object but leaves out who used it.
This tells where, but leaves out the person and action.
This tells when, but leaves out the person and action.

questions.stem: Pretend you saw two pupils carrying books on your first school day. Tell who did what.
hints: Begin with the people you saw.
questions.explanation: A witness could report that two pupils carried books. The report names the actors and their activity.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Describes carrying books as their action.

criteria.description: Identifies the two pupils.
Describes carrying books as their action.

questions.stem: Act out an activity you remember from class. Let a partner describe the people and action.
hints: Choose an action your partner can see.
questions.explanation: Acting out handing out books gives a partner evidence about who handed the books to whom.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Checks the partner’s description against what happened.

criteria.description: Acts out a recognisable past class activity.
Checks the partner’s description against what happened.

questions.stem: A friend says “The hall” when asked what happened at assembly. Ask two questions to improve the story.
hints: A place alone does not describe an event.
questions.explanation: “Who was in the hall?” and “What did they do there?” turn a place name into a report about people.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Asks what the people did.

criteria.description: Asks who was involved.
Asks what the people did.

questions.stem: Ama first washed her hands and then ate. Which action happened earlier?
hints: Listen for the word first.
questions.explanation: The story puts washing before eating. Washing was earlier.
questions.misconception: Eating came after washing in Ama's story.

distractorMisconceptions.Eating the meal: Eating came after washing in Ama's story.
distractorMisconceptions.Finishing the meal: She finished eating after she washed.
distractorMisconceptions.Clearing the plate: Clearing a plate comes after the meal.

questions.stem: Which pair puts an event before a memory of it?
options: We told its story; the match began.
The match ended; we told its story.
We recalled the goal; it had never happened.
We remembered a race that had not started.
hints: An event must happen before it can be remembered.
questions.explanation: After the match ends, its players can tell what happened. A memory looks back.
questions.misconception: The story of this match cannot come before the match itself.

The story of this match cannot come before the match itself.
distractorMisconceptions.We recalled the goal; it had never happe: A goal that never happened cannot be remembered as an event.
distractorMisconceptions.We remembered a race that had not starte: The race must take place before people can recall it.

questions.stem: Place two picture cards in order: children entering a room, then the same children starting their lesson.
hints: Think about how the children reached their seats.
questions.explanation: The children enter before they can sit down and start that lesson.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Gives a reason based on the pictured actions.

criteria.description: Places entering first.
Gives a reason based on the pictured actions.

questions.stem: Make two panels about an activity you completed today. Tell which part came first.
hints: Choose something with a clear beginning.
questions.explanation: A learner might show opening a book, then reading it. The two pictures put the actions in order.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Uses first and then in the correct order.

criteria.description: Shows two connected actions.
Uses first and then in the correct order.

questions.stem: Two recollections say “we planted a seed” and “we showed the growing plant”. Put them in order and explain.
hints: What needed to happen for there to be a plant to show?
questions.explanation: The seed had to be planted before the pupils could show the growing plant. This orders two past human activities.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains the relationship between the actions.

criteria.description: Places planting before showing the growing plant.
Explains the relationship between the actions.

questions.stem: Which is a message about a past class event?
options: We hope to visit a garden.
hints: Look for a visit already made.
questions.explanation: Visited tells us that the class already took the trip. A plan or request does not say it happened.
questions.misconception: A hope tells what we want to happen.

A hope tells what we want to happen.
distractorMisconceptions.Shall we visit a garden?: An invitation suggests a possible trip.
A request for tomorrow refers to a future trip.

questions.stem: Which question asks someone to remember history?
options: What colour do you want next year?
What did you do on your first school day?
What game shall we play later?
hints: Look for a question about an earlier experience.
questions.explanation: A first school day has already happened for a pupil in class. The question invites a memory of that day.
questions.misconception: Choosing for next year is planning.

distractorMisconceptions.What colour do you want next year?: Choosing for next year is planning.
distractorMisconceptions.What will you pack tomorrow?: Packing tomorrow has not happened yet.
distractorMisconceptions.What game shall we play later?: Choosing a later game is a plan.

questions.stem: Tell one thing your class used to do but no longer does. Say how you know about it.
hints: Think of a routine that changed.
questions.explanation: A pupil might remember meeting in another room. Remembering that former routine tells something about the class’s past.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Identifies a memory or person who recalls it.

criteria.description: Names a past class activity.
Identifies a memory or person who recalls it.

questions.stem: Interview a partner about yesterday’s playtime and retell the answer in one sentence.
hints: Listen for the person and the action.
questions.explanation: If the partner says they played a game, report that game. The retelling should follow what the partner said.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Retells the answer without adding an invented action.

criteria.description: Asks about a completed activity.
Retells the answer without adding an invented action.

questions.stem: Tell a short first-day story with two people, one activity and one clue that it happened in the past.
hints: Start with when and who.
questions.explanation: “On my first school day, my sister and I carried my books” names people, an activity and its time in the past.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Uses a clear past-time clue tied to the story.

criteria.description: Identifies the participants and their activity.
Uses a clear past-time clue tied to the story.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.sub_strand: Why and How We Study History
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.1.1. Demonstrate understanding of what history is about and how it is part of everyday life.
indicator.objective: Describe how sources of historical evidence help us find out about past human activities

skills.description: Describe a detail visible in a picture of a past event.
Choose an eyewitness and ask about an experience.
Read a name or date from a written record.
Select and compare sources for a particular question.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: An empty album contains no pictures to examine.
Planning to attend is different from being there.
A classroom door does not record the pupil's date of birth.
Blank pages give no account to compare.

questions.stem: What can show how people looked at a wedding?
hints: Look for a record made at the event.
questions.explanation: The photograph shows people present when it was taken. An empty album shows nobody.
questions.misconception: An empty album contains no pictures to examine.

distractorMisconceptions.An empty album: An empty album contains no pictures to examine.
distractorMisconceptions.A bag bought today: This bag has no stated link to the wedding.
distractorMisconceptions.A wish for a wedding: A wish does not record what anyone saw.

questions.stem: A party photo shows children holding cups. Which detail can you see in it?
hints: Use something your eyes could check.
questions.explanation: The cups are visible. Sound, feelings and arrival time need other evidence.
questions.misconception: A still photo cannot tell how loud a sound was.

A still photo cannot tell how loud a sound was.
Holding a drink does not show whether someone liked it.
The cups do not tell the time of arrival.

questions.stem: Sketch a birthday scene you remember. Mark one detail you remember seeing.
hints: Think of something people did.
questions.explanation: Showing a person cutting a cake records a remembered action that another person could ask about.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Marks a visible detail from the memory.

criteria.description: Shows a celebration activity.
Marks a visible detail from the memory.

questions.stem: Choose two pictures from a class album. Put an earlier picture first using their labels.
hints: Check whether the pictures have dates.
questions.explanation: An earlier date belongs before a later one. Picture size does not tell age.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains which clue supports the order.

criteria.description: Uses the labels to identify the order.
Explains which clue supports the order.

questions.stem: A photograph shows a crowd. A friend says everyone was happy. Explain what the photograph shows and what you would ask.
hints: Separate seeing people from knowing how they felt.
questions.explanation: A photograph can show a group standing together. Asking someone who was there can add what they remember feeling.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Asks for evidence about feelings.

criteria.description: Names a visible feature.
Asks for evidence about feelings.

questions.stem: Who could tell what they saw at last week’s class festival?
options: A pupil who only plans to go
A person who has never heard of it
hints: Who was there?
questions.explanation: A pupil present at the festival can describe a personal memory.
questions.misconception: Planning to attend is different from being there.

distractorMisconceptions.A pupil who only plans to go: Planning to attend is different from being there.
distractorMisconceptions.A visitor arriving next week: Someone arriving next week missed last week's festival.
distractorMisconceptions.A person who has never heard of it: Someone who never heard of it cannot recount what happened there.

questions.stem: Which question asks an elder for evidence about an old celebration?
hints: Ask about an experience already lived.
questions.explanation: Asking what the elder saw invites an account of the earlier event.
questions.misconception: A prediction asks for a guess about the future.

distractorMisconceptions.What might happen tomorrow?: A prediction asks for a guess about the future.
distractorMisconceptions.What colour shall I use?: Choosing a colour does not ask what the elder saw.
distractorMisconceptions.Will you come next week?: A future invitation asks for a plan.

questions.stem: Ask a partner about a celebration they remember. Repeat one detail they gave.
hints: Listen before you retell.
questions.explanation: The partner’s memory is a spoken source. Retelling should preserve the detail they gave.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Repeats the partner’s detail accurately.

criteria.description: Asks about a past celebration.
Repeats the partner’s detail accurately.

questions.stem: A rhyme mentions people singing at a festival. Tell one question you would ask an older singer.
hints: Ask how the singer knows about it.
questions.explanation: Asking when people sang the rhyme helps connect the sung words with events in the past.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Connects the question to the rhyme.

criteria.description: Asks about the earlier festival.
Connects the question to the rhyme.

questions.stem: One child remembers dancing and another remembers drumming at the same party. Explain why you would listen to both.
hints: Think about what different people might notice.
questions.explanation: One account may describe the dancers and another the drummers. Both can add to the story.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Allows that both could have happened.

criteria.description: Identifies the two different activities.
Allows that both could have happened.

questions.stem: Which source helps you find the month of a classmate’s birthday?
options: A picture of the classroom door
hints: Look for names connected to dates.
questions.explanation: A birthday register links a person with a recorded date.
questions.misconception: A classroom door does not record the pupil's date of birth.

distractorMisconceptions.A picture of the classroom door: A classroom door does not record the pupil's date of birth.
distractorMisconceptions.A list of favourite colours: A list of colours has no birthday dates.
distractorMisconceptions.An empty calendar: An empty calendar does not link a date to a person.

questions.stem: A practice register says “Esi — 5 May”. Which detail can you get from the entry?
hints: Read only what the entry gives.
questions.explanation: The entry pairs Esi with 5 May. It gives no details about a party.
questions.misconception: A name and date do not identify a song.

distractorMisconceptions.Esi’s favourite song: A name and date do not identify a song.
distractorMisconceptions.The cake’s colour: A birthday date cannot tell us the cake's colour.
distractorMisconceptions.The party guests: A register entry for one pupil does not list the guests.

questions.stem: Make a practice birthday entry for a made-up pupil. Use a name and date.
hints: Two pieces of information belong together.
questions.explanation: A register can show a name beside a day and month so another person can read the date.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Pairs it with a clear date.

criteria.description: Writes a made-up name.
Pairs it with a clear date.

questions.stem: A birthday card says “Kojo — 8 June”. A copy says “Kojo — 8 July”. Correct the copy using the card.
hints: Compare the months carefully.
questions.explanation: The original card gives 8 June. The changed month is the copying error.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Keeps the child and day unchanged.

criteria.description: Identifies June on the original.
Keeps the child and day unchanged.

questions.stem: Order three practice cards dated 2 May, 4 May and 9 May. Explain how someone could use this record.
hints: Compare days within the same month.
questions.explanation: The dates run from 2 to 4 to 9 May. A class could use them to see whose birthday comes next.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains a use for the ordered record.

criteria.description: Orders the dates correctly.
Explains a use for the ordered record.

questions.stem: Which pair gives two different clues about the same festival?
options: Its photograph and a guest’s memory
A future plan and a blank envelope
hints: Choose records connected to the event.
questions.explanation: A photograph shows visible details. A guest can recall sounds or actions that the photograph may miss.
questions.misconception: Blank pages give no account to compare.

distractorMisconceptions.Two empty pages: Blank pages give no account to compare.
distractorMisconceptions.A future plan and a blank envelope: A plan and an empty envelope do not record the festival.
distractorMisconceptions.Two guesses about next year: Guesses about next year do not describe an earlier event.

questions.stem: A child wants to hear a song from a past celebration. Which record could help most?
options: A still picture of a drum
hints: Which record keeps sound?
questions.explanation: A recording can preserve the sung words or tune. The other records cannot replay it.
questions.misconception: A picture shows the drum but cannot play the song.

distractorMisconceptions.A still picture of a drum: A picture shows the drum but cannot play the song.
distractorMisconceptions.A list of chairs: A list of chairs has no record of the music.
distractorMisconceptions.A blank notebook: A blank notebook contains no record of the song.

questions.stem: Name something an event photograph can show and something a witness can tell.
hints: Think of sight and sound.
questions.explanation: The photograph might show a drum. A witness might recall the sound of the drumming.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Names a detail a witness could add.

criteria.description: Names a visible detail.
Names a detail a witness could add.

questions.stem: Build a little evidence display for a pretend class celebration using a picture and a dated note.
hints: One source can show; another can name or date.
questions.explanation: The picture can show an action and the note can date it. Together they help someone tell the story.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Labels the different clue each offers.

criteria.description: Includes two related sources.
Labels the different clue each offers.

questions.stem: Your group has a birthday photo without a date and a dated guest note. Explain how to check whether they belong to the same party.
hints: Look for a shared person or event description.
questions.explanation: A guest might recognise who is in the picture and what they were doing. Matching details make the connection stronger.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains why the date alone does not prove a match.

criteria.description: Identifies a matching detail to check.
Explains why the date alone does not prove a match.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.4.2. Recount history about their communities.
indicator.objective: State the similarities and differences between the communities where learners live.

skills.description: Name a feature of a community that can be studied.
State a feature shared by two places.
Describe how two communities differ.
Support a comparison with evidence from both places.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: A game pupils plan to invent is a future activity.
Both maps mark a building.
The sketches show sites, not a count of visitors.
One guess gives no evidence from the other site.

questions.stem: What is a community feature pupils might visit to learn about the past?
options: A game they plan to invent
hints: Look for an actual place.
questions.explanation: An old post office is a place in a community. Its building and stories may provide evidence.
questions.misconception: A game pupils plan to invent is a future activity.

distractorMisconceptions.A game they plan to invent: A game pupils plan to invent is a future activity.
distractorMisconceptions.Next week’s homework: A homework task is not a site to visit.
distractorMisconceptions.A wish for a trip: Wishing for a trip does not identify a place to study.

questions.stem: A visitor says “I saw the chief’s palace.” Which detail did the visitor identify?
hints: What kind of thing is a palace?
questions.explanation: A palace is a place. Naming it identifies a feature that another community can be compared with.
questions.misconception: A palace names a place, while a date tells when.

distractorMisconceptions.A festival date: A palace names a place, while a date tells when.
distractorMisconceptions.A person’s birthday: A birthday tells when a person was born.
distractorMisconceptions.A song title: A song title names music, while a palace is a place.

questions.stem: Draw one site in your community and add its name or a spoken label.
hints: Think of somewhere you have seen.
questions.explanation: A labelled drawing lets someone know which local feature the drawing represents.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Names the site correctly using local knowledge.

criteria.description: Depicts an identifiable site.
Names the site correctly using local knowledge.

questions.stem: Tell a classmate how to find one local place a visitor could ask about.
hints: What would help your partner recognise it?
questions.explanation: A local name and a visible feature can help a visitor identify the right place.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Gives a useful distinguishing clue.

criteria.description: Names a site.
Gives a useful distinguishing clue.

questions.stem: Choose two local site cards and arrange them from older to newer using the dates on the cards.
hints: Compare the dates, not the picture sizes.
questions.explanation: The site with the earlier recorded date goes first. Age needs a date or other evidence.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Places the earlier site first.

criteria.description: Reads the supplied dates.
Places the earlier site first.

questions.stem: Two practice maps both show a post office. How are the places alike?
hints: Look for what appears on both maps.
questions.explanation: A post office is shown twice, once in each community. That is a similarity.
questions.misconception: Both maps mark a building.

A shared post office does not show who lives in each place.
A post office is marked on each map.

questions.stem: Which word helps tell a similarity?
hints: Think about a feature shared by two places.
questions.explanation: Both introduces something true of each place being compared.
questions.misconception: Only singles out one case.

questions.stem: Two practice sketches each show trees beside a path. Say one way the scenes are alike.
hints: Look at the two scenes together.
questions.explanation: Both show trees beside a path. A shared feature is a similarity.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Applies the feature to both scenes.

criteria.description: Names the shared trees or path.
Applies the feature to both scenes.

questions.stem: Draw one feature that your community shares with another community discussed in class. Label the two communities.
hints: Recall two labelled examples.
questions.explanation: A drawing can show the same kind of site in two places even if the buildings look different.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Names or identifies the communities being compared.

criteria.description: Shows a feature present in both.
Names or identifies the communities being compared.

questions.stem: Two communities both have a meeting place. What further question could you ask to compare how people use it?
hints: Ask the same question in each place.
questions.explanation: Asking who meets there, or when, allows the answers to be compared fairly.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Seeks information from both communities.

criteria.description: Asks about an activity at the site.
Seeks information from both communities.

questions.stem: One sample sketch shows a wetland; the other shows a forest. What is different?
hints: Use what the sketches actually show.
questions.explanation: The sketches identify two different kinds of place. They give no visitor or family list.
questions.misconception: The sketches show sites, not a count of visitors.

distractorMisconceptions.The number of visitors today: The sketches show sites, not a count of visitors.
distractorMisconceptions.The age of every tree: The sketches do not tell the ages of trees.
distractorMisconceptions.The names of all families: The sketches identify landscapes rather than families.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives a difference?
options: The two pictures are on our desk.
One map shows a chapel; the other shows a palace.
hints: Look for a feature that changes from one picture to the other.
questions.explanation: The first sentence compares a chapel with a palace. The other sentences identify shared or unrelated facts.
questions.misconception: A shared path gives a similarity.

A shared path gives a similarity.
Labels on both drawings give a similarity.
Being on one desk does not compare the sites shown.

questions.stem: Compare a drawing of a wide river with one of a narrow stream. Use one difference you can see.
hints: Describe the water in both pictures.
questions.explanation: One waterway looks wider and the other narrower. The description compares the same feature.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Says which drawing shows each feature.

criteria.description: Names a visible difference.
Says which drawing shows each feature.

questions.stem: Complete this comparison from practice notes: “A has an old chapel. B has a palace.”
hints: Use one fact from each note.
questions.explanation: The notes identify different historical sites in the two communities.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Reports the palace in B.

criteria.description: Reports the chapel in A.
Reports the palace in B.

questions.stem: A child says two communities are completely different because one drawing contains a forest. What else would you check?
hints: Look for both shared and different features.
questions.explanation: You could check for a forest in the other place and for meeting places in both. One picture is only part of the evidence.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Recognises that one difference does not settle every comparison.

criteria.description: Asks about features in the other community.
Recognises that one difference does not settle every comparison.

questions.stem: What helps someone check a comparison of two visited sites?
options: A plan for a future game
hints: Choose records from the places being compared.
questions.explanation: Two labelled sketches let a reader connect the observations with the correct sites.
questions.misconception: One guess gives no evidence from the other site.

distractorMisconceptions.A guess about one site: One guess gives no evidence from the other site.
distractorMisconceptions.A blank paper: A blank sheet records nothing from either visit.
distractorMisconceptions.A plan for a future game: An unrelated future plan does not record the sites.

questions.stem: One picture shows only a chapel door. What can we safely say?
options: That community has no other site.
The chapel is the oldest in Ghana.
hints: Say only what you can see.
questions.explanation: The small view shows a door. It cannot show everything in the community or prove its age.
questions.misconception: One view cannot show all the sites in a community.

One view cannot show all the sites in a community.
A chapel door tells us nothing about every house.
A picture of a door cannot establish a national age record.

questions.stem: Match two site descriptions from your teacher to their labelled pictures. Point to your clues.
hints: Check details such as a doorway, tree or sign.
questions.explanation: A detail repeated in the description and picture helps identify the site.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Identifies a visible clue for each match.

criteria.description: Matches both descriptions.
Identifies a visible clue for each match.

questions.stem: Make a two-part display of communities studied in class. Show one shared and one different feature.
hints: Use the class pictures to check your labels.
questions.explanation: A useful comparison shows what the places have in common as well as one difference supported by the pictures.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Labels a feature that differs.

criteria.description: Depicts a genuine shared feature.
Labels a feature that differs.

questions.stem: A visitor asks whether two sites are the same age. You have sketches but no dates. Give a careful answer and name a source you could ask for.
hints: Think about what a drawing cannot tell by itself.
questions.explanation: Appearance can suggest a question. Dates or a reliable local account are needed before you give an age order.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Suggests a dated record or knowledgeable person.

criteria.description: Explains that the sketches alone do not settle age.
Suggests a dated record or knowledgeable person.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B1.2.3.1. Demonstrate understanding of why Ghana used to be called the ‘Gold Coast’.
indicator.objective: Explain why, in the past, Ghana was known as the Gold Coast.

skills.description: Identify Gold Coast as a former name of Ghana.
Connect the words in the name with gold and the coast.
Use a trade clue to explain the historical name.
Distinguish the earlier and later names for the country.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Cape Coast names a town, rather than the country's former name.
Iron is a different metal from the one in the name.

questions.stem: Prepare a name-and-field card for a Ghanaian in this lesson whose work you admire.
hints: Use a specific contribution rather than only saying famous.
questions.explanation: A complete card might say Theodosia Okoh — national flag. The field explains the reason for inclusion.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Gives the correct field or national symbol.

criteria.description: Names a contributor from the lesson.
Gives the correct field or national symbol.

questions.stem: Sort four name cards from this lesson under four different contribution labels. Explain one match to the teacher.
hints: Read each heading before placing its person.
questions.explanation: Matching people with their actual fields shows how different kinds of work contribute to national life.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Justifies one match by naming the contribution.

criteria.description: Correctly sorts four supplied pairs.
Justifies one match by naming the contribution.

questions.stem: Introduce a class gallery featuring one national symbol, one sport and one creative field. Name a contributor for each.
hints: Choose a symbol first; then choose sport and creative work.
questions.explanation: For example, Okoh represents the flag, Baba Yara football and Amu music. Each label gives a different kind of contribution.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Connects each to the requested kind of contribution.

criteria.description: Identifies three appropriate people.
Connects each to the requested kind of contribution.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B1.3.1.1 Show understanding of Europeans who came to Ghana
indicator.objective: Explore which Europeans came to Ghana

skills.description: Identify European countries named in the curriculum.
Match country names with the names for people from those places.
Use map labels to trace the start and end of a route.
Choose evidence to investigate an arrival or settlement.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Denmark belongs with the word Danish.
Swedish points to Sweden.
A birthday list records dates, not country locations.
Spelling length gives no time information.

questions.stem: Which country named in the lesson is linked with Portuguese visitors?
hints: Look at the country name that goes with Portuguese.
questions.explanation: Portuguese people come from Portugal. Portugal is among the countries named in the lesson.
questions.misconception: Denmark belongs with the word Danish.

distractorMisconceptions.Denmark: Denmark belongs with the word Danish.
distractorMisconceptions.France: France belongs with the word French.
distractorMisconceptions.Sweden: Sweden belongs with the word Swedish.

questions.stem: Which country in the lesson is linked with Danish visitors?
hints: Say the people name and think of its country.
questions.explanation: Danish is the people name linked with Denmark.
questions.misconception: Germany belongs with the word German.

distractorMisconceptions.Germany: Germany belongs with the word German.
distractorMisconceptions.Norway: Norway belongs with the word Norwegian.
distractorMisconceptions.Netherlands: The Netherlands belongs with the word Dutch.

questions.stem: Name two European countries listed in the class lesson about arrivals.
hints: Use the list your teacher read.
questions.explanation: Portugal and Sweden are two examples. Britain, France, Germany, Denmark, Norway and the Netherlands also appear.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Names a different listed country.

criteria.description: Names one listed country.
Names a different listed country.

questions.stem: From cards marked France, Sweden, Ghana and school, choose two European country names in the lesson.
hints: Find two places named among the European countries of origin.
questions.explanation: France and Sweden both appear in the list. Ghana names the place being studied as the destination.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Selects Sweden.

criteria.description: Selects France.
Selects Sweden.

questions.stem: A child labels all European visitors “from Portugal”. Use two examples to improve the label.
hints: Check how many country names the lesson gives.
questions.explanation: Portugal was one country of origin. Visitors from other named countries, such as Denmark, also came.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Explains that visitors came from more than one country.

criteria.description: Names Portugal and a different listed country.
Explains that visitors came from more than one country.

questions.stem: Which label means people from France?
hints: Match the words for people with their home country.
questions.explanation: French identifies people from France.
questions.misconception: Swedish points to Sweden.

questions.stem: A practice card says “from Norway”. Which people does the card describe?
hints: Focus on the country of origin.
questions.explanation: Norwegians are people from Norway. Norway appears in the lesson’s list.
questions.misconception: Danes come from Denmark.

distractorMisconceptions.Dutch people: Dutch people come from the Netherlands.

questions.stem: Pair Sweden and Germany with the words Swedish and German.
hints: Read each country name aloud.
questions.explanation: Swedish links to Sweden and German to Germany. The first word in each pair names a country.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Matches Germany and German.

criteria.description: Matches Sweden and Swedish.
Matches Germany and German.

questions.stem: A visitor card says “Dutch”. Tell your partner the related country name and how the two labels differ.
hints: Check the country list for the Netherlands.
questions.explanation: Dutch is a word for people from the Netherlands. The Netherlands is the country name.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Distinguishes a people label from a country label.

criteria.description: Names the Netherlands.
Distinguishes a people label from a country label.

questions.stem: Make two picture-free name labels for a class map: one for people from Britain and one for people from Portugal.
hints: Connect each group label with its place of origin.
questions.explanation: The labels British—Britain and Portuguese—Portugal can accompany their places on a map.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Correctly links Portuguese with Portugal.

criteria.description: Correctly links British with Britain.
Correctly links Portuguese with Portugal.

questions.stem: What would best help a pupil locate the countries of origin?
hints: Look for a source that shows places.
questions.explanation: A labelled world map shows where countries are. A list of birthdays cannot locate them.
questions.misconception: A birthday list records dates, not country locations.

distractorMisconceptions.A birthday list: A birthday list records dates, not country locations.
distractorMisconceptions.A shopping bag: A shopping bag is not a guide to a country's location.
distractorMisconceptions.A class bell: A bell cannot show where a journey began.

questions.stem: On a practice map, an arrow starts in Europe and ends at Ghana. What does its starting end show?
hints: Follow the arrow from the starting place.
questions.explanation: The starting end represents where the journey began. A map arrow alone does not give a date.
questions.misconception: The tail of an arrow marks where a route begins, not when it ends.

distractorMisconceptions.A date of arrival: The tail of an arrow marks where a route begins, not when it ends.
distractorMisconceptions.The name of every ship: An arrow on a map cannot name all the ships.
distractorMisconceptions.How long the visit lasted: A map arrow alone does not measure time spent visiting.

questions.stem: Find Ghana and one European country named in the lesson on a labelled world map.
hints: Read the labels before you point.
questions.explanation: Pointing to the two places separates the destination from a country of origin.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Identifies the selected European country.

criteria.description: Identifies Ghana.
Identifies the selected European country.

questions.stem: Sketch a simple journey diagram from one listed European country to Ghana. Add labels.
hints: A journey diagram needs a start and an end.
questions.explanation: An arrow from France to Ghana, for example, labels origin and destination without pretending to trace an exact route.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Shows the direction towards Ghana.

criteria.description: Labels the chosen country and Ghana.
Shows the direction towards Ghana.

questions.stem: A partner says the country closest to Ghana on a map must have arrived first. Explain what else the class needs.
hints: Think about what a map shows and what a timeline shows.
questions.explanation: Distance tells where places are, while a date or reliable arrival account can help establish who came earlier.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Suggests dated information or an account about arrival.

criteria.description: Distinguishes distance from arrival order.
Suggests dated information or an account about arrival.

questions.stem: Which clue is most useful for ordering two arrivals?
options: The number of letters in each name
hints: Look for information about time.
questions.explanation: Comparing arrival dates lets the class place the earlier event first.
questions.misconception: Spelling length gives no time information.

distractorMisconceptions.The number of letters in each name: Spelling length gives no time information.
distractorMisconceptions.The colour of the map: Map colour does not put visits in order.
distractorMisconceptions.The height of the display: Display height does not date a visit.

questions.stem: Where could the class ask about an early settlement?
options: A museum with records about the site
hints: Choose a source about that place’s past.
questions.explanation: A museum may hold accounts or objects connected to the site. The source still needs to be checked.
questions.misconception: A blank card contains no evidence about the settlement.

distractorMisconceptions.An empty birthday card: A blank card contains no evidence about the settlement.
distractorMisconceptions.A list of tomorrow’s games: A list of future games does not record old places.
distractorMisconceptions.An unlabelled pencil: A pencil without a label cannot identify the early settlement.

questions.stem: Ask a question that could help you learn where one named European group first settled.
hints: Include who and where.
questions.explanation: “Where did the Danish visitors first settle?” is a question for a knowledgeable guide or historical record.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Asks about a place of early settlement.

criteria.description: Names a group from the curriculum.
Asks about a place of early settlement.

questions.stem: Use two dated arrival cards supplied by your teacher. Put the earlier arrival first and point to the evidence.
hints: Work from the years on the cards.
questions.explanation: The smaller earlier year goes first. The order of the names in a printed list alone is not enough.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Uses their dates to justify the order.

criteria.description: Orders the supplied cards correctly.
Uses their dates to justify the order.

questions.stem: Two class sources give different arrival orders. Explain how your group could check the claim before making a gallery label.
hints: Ask what dates or accounts each source actually gives.
questions.explanation: Checking the dates against an appropriate historical account is stronger than guessing from a country’s place on a map.
questions.misconception: A response may overlook this detail: Proposes consulting a relevant source before labelling.

criteria.description: Identifies which group or date needs checking.
Proposes consulting a relevant source before labelling.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B1.6.1.1. Demonstrate understanding of the presidents that have ruled Ghana since 1960
indicator.objective: Identify the Presidents Ghana has had since 1960

skills.description: Identify the person shown using the name on a reliable portrait label.
Read the years that belong to one president’s time in office.
Use a dated class album to place presidents in order.
Make and check a gallery entry that helps another pupil identify a president.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recognition, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Reading a portrait's position as its date.
Mixing up birth years and terms of office.
Joining a name and portrait without checking their captions.

questions.stem: Which part of a labelled portrait tells you who the president is?
hints: Look for words that tell who is shown.
questions.explanation: Read the name beside the portrait. Frame colour, size and number do not name the person.
questions.misconception: Treating a display feature as a person's name.

distractorMisconceptions.The frame colour: Treating a display feature as a person's name.
distractorMisconceptions.The paper size: Treating a display feature as a person's name.
distractorMisconceptions.The gallery number: Treating a display feature as a person's name.

questions.stem: With your teacher, open a labelled album of Ghana’s presidents. Point to the first president and say his name.
hints: Look for the label for the start of the republic in 1960.
questions.explanation: Use the first-president label to find the portrait. Say the name that belongs to it.

criteria.description: Finds the portrait for the first president.
Names the person on its label.

questions.misconception: Naming the first picture on any page without checking its label.

questions.stem: A class card has a name, a start year and an end year. Which two details show the person's time as president?
options: Card number and date of birth
hints: Look for when the work began and finished.
questions.explanation: The start year marks taking office. The end year marks leaving office.
questions.misconception: Using a birth date as the start of a presidency.

distractorMisconceptions.Name and card number: Using a birth date as the start of a presidency.
distractorMisconceptions.Card number and date of birth: Using a birth date as the start of a presidency.
distractorMisconceptions.Name and date of birth: Using a birth date as the start of a presidency.

questions.stem: Our class is making the presidents’ album for the years 1960 to 2016. Which year goes at the beginning?
hints: Read the years from earlier to later.
questions.explanation: The album starts in 1960. The other date marks the end of this class enquiry.
questions.misconception: Reversing the first and last years of the enquiry.

questions.stem: You have a checked picture card for the gallery. Where will a visitor look for the president’s name?
options: On the back of the shelf
On the label by the picture
hints: Think of what the visitor can read beside the portrait.
questions.explanation: Place the name beside the matching picture. A visitor can then identify the person it shows.
questions.misconception: Confusing a list of visitors with names on the portraits.

distractorMisconceptions.On the back of the shelf: Confusing a list of visitors with names on the portraits.
distractorMisconceptions.On the classroom clock: Confusing a list of visitors with names on the portraits.
distractorMisconceptions.On the list of visitors: Confusing a list of visitors with names on the portraits.

questions.stem: Ask a partner to read a president’s name from your class album. Find the portrait and show how you checked it.
hints: Match the spoken name to the words beside a picture.
questions.explanation: A spoken name gives you a clue. The full name on the portrait card confirms the match.

criteria.description: Selects the matching portrait.
Checks the full name with the album.

questions.misconception: Matching only the first part of a name.

questions.stem: Two portraits have been taken off a display. What would help you put their name cards back correctly?
hints: Which item links a face with its name?
questions.explanation: A captioned album shows each portrait with a name. Use that link to replace each card.
questions.misconception: Using the frame to identify the person.

distractorMisconceptions.The height of the table: Using the frame to identify the person.
distractorMisconceptions.The colour of the wall: Using the frame to identify the person.
distractorMisconceptions.The price of the frames: Using the frame to identify the person.

questions.stem: Pick a president from your class album. Say the name and read the year that person began serving.
hints: Find the date marked as the start.
questions.explanation: Read the name first. Then follow the same row to its start year.

criteria.description: Reads a president’s name.
Gives the matching start year from that entry.

questions.misconception: Reading a year from the next person's row.

questions.stem: A label has spaces called Born, Took office and Left office. Where would you put the year a president stopped serving?
hints: Listen for the word that means finished the job.
questions.explanation: The end of the time in office goes in the space called Left office. A birth year tells a different part of the person's life.
questions.misconception: Confusing the end of service with its beginning.

distractorMisconceptions.Took office: Confusing the end of service with its beginning.
distractorMisconceptions.Born: A birth year tells when someone was born.
distractorMisconceptions.On the picture frame: The frame holds the picture. The labelled end date records when service finished.

questions.stem: Choose two different presidents in the class album. Put the one who first took office earlier on the left.
hints: Check when each first took office.
questions.explanation: Compare the two start years. Order the portraits by those years and read the names in that order.

criteria.description: Orders two distinct presidents by first start years.
Names both in that order.

questions.misconception: Ordering portraits by their size.

questions.stem: A gallery needs the person who served first. Which way should the class sort the name cards?
hints: What would show that one person began earlier?
questions.explanation: The starting years place the presidents in time. A shorter name or a larger picture does not tell who served first.
questions.misconception: Assuming alphabetical order gives the order of service.

distractorMisconceptions.By length of name: Assuming alphabetical order gives the order of service.
distractorMisconceptions.By colour of paper: Assuming alphabetical order gives the order of service.
distractorMisconceptions.By size of picture: Assuming alphabetical order gives the order of service.

questions.stem: Draw a small display card for one person in the presidents’ album. Add the name below the drawing.
hints: Keep the album open beside your paper.
questions.explanation: Choose one labelled portrait. Copy the name from that entry onto the card so another pupil can identify it.

criteria.description: Represents one selected president.
Adds the correct matching name, by writing or dictating.

questions.misconception: Using the artist’s name as the caption.

questions.stem: Cover the name on one album picture. Name the president, then uncover the caption and say what you found.
hints: Remember a portrait you have already studied.
questions.explanation: Make a first identification. Read the checked caption to confirm or correct the name.

criteria.description: Identifies or corrects the president’s name.
Uses the caption to check.

questions.misconception: Sticking with a first guess after a label shows a different name.

questions.stem: Use the class album to make a name card for one former president with the years that person began and ended a term.
hints: Read both dates on the same entry.
questions.explanation: Match one name to one term. Put the starting year first and the ending year second.

criteria.description: Matches the two dates to the chosen name and term.
Puts the dates in the correct order.

questions.misconception: Combining the start of one person's term with another person's end year.

questions.stem: Find three named presidents in a class timeline. Hide the timeline, arrange their cards, then use it to check your order.
hints: Use the dates when they first took office.
questions.explanation: The earliest start belongs first. Compare the next two and check the finished row against the timeline.

criteria.description: Places three names in order of first taking office.
Checks and, if needed, corrects the row.

questions.misconception: Treating the last card picked as the last person to serve.

questions.stem: A visitor points to one president in your class gallery. Introduce that person by name and say when they served.
hints: Read the picture label and its dates together.
questions.explanation: Use the caption to identify the person. Read the matching period of service from the same display.

criteria.description: Names the person shown.
Gives the matching time in office.

questions.misconception: Giving dates from a neighbouring display.

questions.stem: A card says only “President”. A friend needs to find this same person in another album. What would help most?
hints: What could the friend look for in both albums?
questions.explanation: Several people have held this office. A full personal name gives the friend a way to match the person across both albums.
questions.misconception: Assuming a title identifies just one person across time.

distractorMisconceptions.Use a bigger card: Assuming a title identifies just one person across time.
distractorMisconceptions.Add the writer’s name: Assuming a title identifies just one person across time.
distractorMisconceptions.Use the same ink colour: Assuming a title identifies just one person across time.

questions.stem: A partner covers the name on a gallery card but leaves the years of service. Find the name in a dated class album and check the picture too.
hints: Look for a matching pair of years before checking the portrait.
questions.explanation: Match the period of service to an album entry. Check that its portrait matches and read the name aloud.

criteria.description: Uses both years to locate the matching entry.
Checks the portrait and gives the name.

questions.misconception: Deciding from a single date without checking the other clue.

questions.stem: The first portrait on a wall may be the last one the class put up. How can you find who served first? Show the name in your class album.
hints: Think about the difference between hanging up a picture and taking office.
questions.explanation: Look at the start years in the album. Identify the earliest president in the set and say the name; the wall order alone cannot tell you.

criteria.description: Identifies the earliest president in the chosen set by name.
Explains the choice using a date or a dated timeline.

questions.misconception: Treating the order of hanging pictures as historical order.

questions.stem: A partner swaps two name labels on your presidents’ gallery. Repair the display using a checked album and explain one change.
hints: Compare each picture with its entry before moving the labels.
questions.explanation: Find both portraits in the album. Move each name beneath its own portrait and point to the match that guided you.

criteria.description: Restores both matching labels.
Shows the album evidence for one correction.

questions.misconception: Correcting one label and leaving the other attached to the wrong portrait.

uncertain: Printed page 8 sets a 1960–2016 enquiry and calls for a labelled class gallery. It does not supply the portraits or list the officeholders and tenures. Name and tenure performances use a teacher-provided album.
